extraction.name: ChartQA
extraction.description: A large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries.
extraction.creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four different online sources to ensure variety in visual styles and topics.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Underlying data tables were not available for the Pew dataset, so only chart images were crawled.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Statista (statista.com), The Pew research (pewresearch.org), Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org), and Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or OECD (oecd.org)
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions were automatically generated from human-written chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Invalid questions were filtered out using a heuristic that checks if the answer can be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was also manually cleaned to remove invalid questions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers provided two questions (compositional and visual) with answers for each chart. Another annotator then answered the same questions. If answers exactly matched, they were considered correct; otherwise, they were manually checked to select the final correct answer.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. When accounting for typos and lexical variations on a 500-sample subset, agreement was 78.55%.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The models trained on this dataset could potentially be abused to mislead the public regarding chart contents and implications.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The machine-generated questions may include invalid, incomplete, or unanswerable questions due to domain mismatch between training and test data.

name.evidence: ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning

description.evidence: we present a large-scale benchmark covering 9.6K human-written questions as well as 23.1K questions generated from human-written chart summaries.

url.evidence: Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/vis-nlp/ChartQA

creator.evidence: Ahmed Masryº, Do Xuan Long¹, Jia Qing Tan¹, Shafiq Joty¹¶, Enamul Hoqueº

rai:dataCollection.evidence: we crawled charts from four different sources: (i) Statista... (ii) The Pew research... (iii) Our World In Data... (iv) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: we crawled charts from four different sources... we designed an AMT task... we also generated another 23,111 questions automatically from human-written chart summaries using a T5 model

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: For the Pew dataset, we only crawled chart images since the underlying data tables are not available.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: we crawled charts from four different sources: (i) Statista (statista.com)... (ii) The Pew research (pewresearch.org)... (iii) Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org)... (iv) Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development or OECD (oecd.org)

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: we also generated another 23,111 questions automatically from human-written chart summaries using a T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020)

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: we filter out the question if the answer cannot be found in the chart data table... we manually cleaned the test set of the machine generated dataset by removing invalid questions.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: we asked the crowdworkers to focus on two types of questions for each chart image: compositional and visual questions... For each chart, the workers provide two questions with the answers. The same questions are then answered by another annotator. If both workers’ answers exactly match, we consider the answer to be correct. Otherwise, we manually check the answers to select the final correct answer.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: we designed an AMT task (see A.1 for details) in which we asked the crowdworkers

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Overall, the agreement between the crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. However, such exact match does not consider typos or lexical variations... we have also manually checked the agreement on 500 random samples and found the agreement to be much higher (78.55%)

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: For each chart, the workers provide two questions with the answers. The same questions are then answered by another annotator.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: we also generated another 23,111 questions automatically from human-written chart summaries using a T5 model (Raffel et al., 2020)

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Our models can be abused to mislead the public about the charts content and implications.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: However, the T5 question generation model may still generate invalid questions because of the mismatch in training and test domains. We notice that some questions are either incomplete or not answerable from the chart

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: We randomly split both of the human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine generated (ChartQA-M) QA pairs into train, validation, and test sets
